title: The Word who pitched his tent among us
sum: John begins before the beginning. Before anything was made, the Word already was: with God, and himself God. Through him everything came to exist, and in him was the life that is the light of all people. Then the Word enters the world he made, is turned away by his own, and gives the right to become God's children to all who accept him. "The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (1:14). No one has seen God, but the only one, himself God, has made him known (1:18).

The rest of the chapter turns that hymn into a story told over several days. John the Baptist refuses every title the Jerusalem delegation offers him and points away from himself to "the Lamb of God", "the one who takes the world's sin away" (1:29). Two of his disciples follow Jesus, and one witness leads to another: Andrew finds Simon, Jesus finds Philip, Philip finds Nathanael. Each gives Jesus a new title (Rabbi, Messiah, the one Moses wrote about, Son of God, the King of Israel), and Jesus promises a greater sight: heaven open over the Son of Man.
readings: Read as theology

The prologue (1:1–18) is the lens for the whole Gospel. It tells readers in advance who Jesus is, so that every scene after it is full of irony: characters argue about where he comes from, while readers already know he came from the Father's side. For the churches it became the central text for the doctrine that Christ is truly God and truly human.
Read as history

The second half of the chapter preserves old memories: that Jesus' first followers came from the circle of John the Baptist, that they included Andrew, Peter and Philip from Bethsaida, and that John baptized at a Bethany across the Jordan. The other Gospels tell a different call story by the lake (Mark 1:16–20); the two may describe a first meeting and a later call.
Read alongside Genesis

"In the beginning" repeats the first words of Genesis, and light, darkness, life and creation through God's word follow. Some readers count the days of 1:19–2:1 as a new creation week, and Jacob's ladder (Genesis 28:12) stands behind 1:51. The new beginning is the Word entering his own creation.

views.H: The Baptist's movement was large enough for the Jerusalem leaders to investigate it, and Josephus describes John and his baptism independently (Antiquities 18.116–119). Bethany beyond the Jordan is placed by most at Wadi el-Kharrar, east of the river near Jericho; some prefer Batanea in the north (Riesner), which would fit a short trip to Galilee in 1:43. The tenth hour, the fig tree and Bethsaida are the kind of small details that suggest local knowledge.
views.C: Many critical scholars think the prologue adapts an early Christian hymn, with prose lines about John the Baptist (1:6–8, 15) added to it, perhaps to correct people who honored John too highly. Bultmann argued that the hymn came from a Baptist group; few follow him now. Others hold the prologue was written as an overture to the finished Gospel. The calling of the disciples is told quite differently from Mark, and scholars debate whether John knew Mark's version.
views.L: The prologue works like an overture, introducing the Gospel's key words: life, light, darkness, world, believe, testimony, glory, truth. Then the story enacts it. John testifies (1:6–8 and 1:19–34), the world does not know him (1:10 and 1:26), some receive him (1:12 and 1:37–49), and the only one who has seen God promises that others will see (1:18 and 1:51). Disciples are made by being told "Come and see" (1:39, 46).
views.J: Jewish readers would hear Genesis 1 and Wisdom literature: Wisdom was with God at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31), came to dwell in Israel (Sirach 24:8) and was sometimes turned away (1 Enoch 42). Philo of Alexandria called the Logos God's firstborn and even a "second god" while staying a Jew, and the Aramaic Targums speak of God's "Memra" (Word) acting in the world. Daniel Boyarin argues that the prologue is itself a Jewish text, a midrash on Genesis, before it became a Christian doctrine. "The Jews" in 1:19 are simply the Jerusalem authorities.
views.T: The prologue was read at Christmas and, in the Latin Church, at the end of every Mass for centuries ("the Last Gospel"). At Nicaea (325) and after, the church read 1:1 and 1:14 as proof that the Son is fully God and fully human; Arius and his followers read "God" in 1:1 in a lesser sense. The Lamb of God (1:29) entered the liturgy as the Agnus Dei sung before Communion.

deep.b:
John never explains logos; he assumes his readers will hear several things at once. In Greek philosophy since Heraclitus the Logos was the reason or order running through the universe, and the Stoics called it divine. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish thinker of Jesus' day, blended this with the Bible: the Logos was God's image, his firstborn, the instrument through which he made the world, and the high priest between God and creation (On the Creation 24–25; On Dreams 1.215).

The Bible itself gave a closer background. God created by speaking (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6), and his word goes out and does his will (Isaiah 55:11). Jewish Wisdom was with God at creation and came to live among Israel (Proverbs 8:22–31; Sirach 24:8; Wisdom of Solomon 9:1–2, 9). The Aramaic Targums often say God acted by his "Memra" (Word), as when the Memra of the LORD made a covenant or appeared.

What is new in John is 1:14: the Word "became flesh." No Greek philosopher and no Jewish writer had said that Wisdom or the Logos became a human being. That is the claim the rest of the Gospel unfolds.

At 1:18 the oldest Greek manuscripts (Papyrus 66, Papyrus 75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) call Jesus "only God" or "the only God" (monogenēs theos), while most later manuscripts read "the only Son" (monogenēs huios), which sounds more natural and matches 3:16, 18. Most editors print "God", because it is older and harder; Bart Ehrman argues it was changed by orthodox scribes, and others answer that "Son" is the easier, likelier change. Either way, the verse ends the prologue as it began: the Word who is God reveals God (see the variant).

At 1:34 most manuscripts have John call Jesus "the Son of God", but Papyrus 106 (probably), Sinaiticus' first hand and some Old Latin and Old Syriac witnesses read "the Chosen One of God". This translation follows SBLGNT in printing "Chosen One", since a scribe was more likely to change it to the familiar title than the other way; it would echo the servant whom God chose and on whom he put his Spirit (Isaiah 42:1). NA28 prints "Son of God".

John marks the days: the delegation (1:19–28), "the following day" (1:29), "the day after that" (1:35), "the day after" (1:43), and then "on the third day" (2:1). If 1:39–42 runs into another day, the count reaches seven. Some modern interpreters, such as M.-É. Boismard, have seen a new creation week (Brown discusses the idea), ending with the wedding at Cana where Jesus "made his glory visible" (2:11). Others count six days, matching the six days before the glory appeared on Sinai (Exodus 24:16). John does not total the days, so the pattern is a suggestion the reader may notice, not a point the text insists on.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the chapter acts out its prologue
deep.b: This is my own way of putting it, though several commentators have noticed parts of the pattern. The story in 1:19–51 seems to walk through the prologue line by line. A man sent from God comes to testify (1:6–8), and the Baptist testifies (1:19–34). He is not the light (1:8), and he says "I am not" three times (1:20–21). The world did not know him (1:10), and John says, "In the middle of you stands someone whom you people do not know" (1:26). All who accepted him (1:12) are acted out by Andrew, Peter, Philip and Nathanael. And the only one who has explained God (1:18) ends the chapter promising that his followers will see heaven open (1:51). If this is deliberate, the prologue is not abstract theology placed before a story; it is the story told in advance.

echoes: Genesis 1:1–5; Genesis 28:10–17; Exodus 33:18–23; Exodus 34:6; Exodus 40:34–35; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; Proverbs 8:22–31; Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 53:7; Malachi 4:5; Sirach 24:8; Mark 1:2–11; Mark 1:16–20; Matthew 16:17–18; 1 John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:15–17; Hebrews 1:1–3; Revelation 19:13

settings.by: The Gospel's narrator, writing for his readers (perhaps adapting an early hymn)
settings.why: To tell readers at the start who Jesus is, the Word who was with God and was God and became flesh, so that they read every later scene knowing more than the characters do. It also answers the hope of Wisdom and Torah: what Moses gave was good, but grace and truth arrive in Jesus Christ.
settings.readers: For believers late in the first century, perhaps including Jewish believers in tension with synagogue leaders, as many scholars think, the prologue claimed that their faith in Jesus was not a break with Israel's God but the fullest meeting with him. It also gave them words for worship.
views: Many scholars (Brown, Schnackenburg) think 1:1–5, 10–12, 14 and 16 come from a hymn sung by Christians, with prose added about John the Baptist.
Others (Carson, Barrett) think the evangelist wrote the prologue himself as the introduction to his finished Gospel, which it summarizes.

settings.what: John's testimony to the Jerusalem delegation
settings.to: Priests and Levites sent by "the Jews of Jerusalem", connected with the Pharisees
settings.when: at Bethany beyond the Jordan, while John was baptizing crowds
settings.why: The authorities were checking whether John claimed a role in the end-time hopes: the Messiah, Elijah, or the Prophet like Moses. John refuses every title, calls himself only a voice from Isaiah 40:3, and turns their attention to someone they do not know.
settings.readers: Some of John's readers may have known groups that honored the Baptist highly (Acts 18:25; 19:1–7). The scene keeps his honor as a witness while making clear he was not the Messiah.

settings.to: Those around him, probably his disciples and the crowds coming for baptism
settings.when: the day after the delegation, as Jesus came toward him
settings.why: To identify the one he had been sent to reveal to Israel, and to report the sign God had given him: the Spirit coming down and staying on Jesus. The titles (Lamb, one who baptizes in the Spirit, Chosen One or Son of God) tell hearers what Jesus will do: take away sin and give the Spirit.
settings.readers: Readers who knew how the story ended would hear in "Lamb" the Passover lambs slaughtered as Jesus died (19:14, 36).
views: Many link the Lamb to the Passover lamb, since John dates Jesus' death to the day the lambs were killed (19:14, 36).
The servant led like a lamb
Others hear Isaiah's servant who went like a lamb to slaughter and bore others' sins (Isaiah 53:7, 12).
Some (Dodd) point to the warrior lamb of Jewish apocalyptic writing and Revelation, which the Baptist might have meant as the coming judge.

settings.by: Jesus, John the Baptist, Andrew, Philip and Nathanael
settings.to: Each other: two of John's disciples, Simon, Philip and Nathanael
settings.when: over two or three days near the Jordan and on the way to Galilee
settings.why: Each conversation is an invitation. Jesus asks what the two are looking for and tells them to come and see; each new follower tells someone else. Nathanael's doubt about Nazareth is met by Jesus' knowledge of him and a promise of greater things.
settings.readers: For later believers, who could not meet Jesus in person, these scenes showed how faith spreads: by one person's testimony and an invitation to see for oneself (compare 20:29–31).

traditions.q: What does "the Word was God" (1:1) mean: is the Son fully God, equal with the Father?
views: Yes. The Word is God in the full sense, of one substance with the Father, eternally begotten, as the Nicene Creed confesses; the Word became flesh without ceasing to be God.
Yes. The fathers, especially Athanasius against Arius, read 1:1 as the Son's full divinity and eternal being with the Father. The Son is "God from God, Light from Light".
Yes, as the Nicene and Athanasian Creeds teach. Luther preached that "the Word was with God" shows two persons, and "the Word was God" one divine being.
Yes. The Son is of one substance, power and eternity with the Father. Calvin read 1:1 as teaching both the Son's distinct person and his eternal deity.
Trinitarian Pentecostals, such as the Assemblies of God, confess the Son as fully God.

Oneness Pentecostals, such as the United Pentecostal Church International, also say the Word is fully God but deny three persons: the Word is God's own self-expression, and Jesus is the one God made flesh.

No. The Word is a mighty spirit creature, the first thing God made. Their New World Translation reads "the Word was a god", arguing from the missing Greek article that the Word is divine in quality but not Almighty God.

The Word is Jesus Christ in his life before birth, a divine being, God the Son, but a separate being from God the Father, one with him in purpose rather than in substance. The Joseph Smith Translation, which Latter-day Saints receive as inspired, rewrites 1:1 to say that the gospel was preached through the Son, and that the Son was with God and was of God.

title: Wine at a wedding, a whip in the temple
sum: Two scenes open Jesus' public life. At a village wedding in Cana the wine runs out. Jesus' mother tells him, and though he says his hour has not come, he has the servants fill six large stone jars, used for Jewish purity washings, with water. What they carry to the man running the feast is the best wine of the whole celebration. John calls it the beginning of the signs: Jesus "He made his glory visible, and his disciples believed in him" (2:11).

Then at Passover Jesus drives the animal sellers and money changers out of the temple grounds with a whip of cords. When the authorities ask for a sign, he says, "Tear this temple down, and within three days I will raise it" (2:19). They think of the building, forty-six years in the making; John explains that he meant his body. Both scenes say the same thing in different ways: what the old purity rites and the temple pointed to is now present in Jesus.
readings: Read as signs

John calls the miracles "signs": acts that point beyond themselves. The jars for purity washings become the source of rich wine, which the prophets promised for the days of God's renewal (Amos 9:13–14). The cleared temple points to a new temple, Jesus' risen body.
Read as history

The temple scene is in all four Gospels, but the other three put it at the end of Jesus' ministry, as a cause of his arrest. Historians ask whether John moved it, whether the Synoptics did, or whether it happened twice. The Cana wedding is told only by John.

views.H: The "forty-six years" (2:20) fits Josephus' dating of Herod's temple rebuilding from about 20/19 BC, which puts this Passover around AD 27–28. Stone jars like those at Cana have been found across Judea and Galilee: stone did not become ritually impure, so households used it for purity water. Animal selling probably took place in the huge outer court Herod had built, the Royal Portico, and the money changers exchanged coins for Tyrian shekels to pay the temple tax.
views.C: Most critical scholars think the temple incident happened once, near the end of Jesus' life, and that John moved it forward for theological reasons, to set the cross over the whole Gospel. A minority (Robinson, and others) think John's order is historical. The Cana story is often traced to the "Signs Source" (Fortna), since it is numbered as the first sign (2:11; 4:54).
views.L: The two scenes form a pair at the start of the ministry: a private sign in Galilee and a public sign in Jerusalem, a feast and a festival, water and the temple. Both contain misunderstandings and an "hour" or a "three days" that points ahead to the cross and resurrection. Both end with disciples believing (2:11, 22).
views.J: Jewish readers would see in the Cana jars the careful purity practice of Galilean and Judean families, which archaeology confirms. Jesus' anger at turning "my Father's house" into a market echoes Zechariah's hope that there would be no traders in the house of the LORD on that day (Zechariah 14:21). Protest against temple practice was not anti-Jewish; the Qumran community and some prophets criticized the temple leaders too.
views.T: Christian tradition has read Cana as Christ's blessing on marriage (the Anglican and Catholic wedding services mention it) and as a sign of the Eucharist, where wine becomes the gift of Christ. Catholic and Orthodox readers stress Mary's intercession: "Whatever he says to you, do it" (2:5). The temple scene has been read as a warning against turning worship into business.

deep.h: Did Jesus clear the temple once or twice?
deep.b:
Matthew, Mark and Luke place the temple action in Jesus' last week (Mark 11:15–18); John places it at the first Passover. There are three main answers. John moved it: most critical scholars think so, arguing that John placed it first as a headline, so the whole ministry is read in the light of the cross and the new temple. The Synoptics moved it: since Mark's outline has only one trip to Jerusalem, any Jerusalem event had to come at the end; John's more detailed calendar may be right (John A. T. Robinson). It happened twice: many traditional interpreters, among them Augustine and many evangelical scholars such as Carson, hold that Jesus did it at both ends of his ministry, since the words and details differ (in John, a whip and a saying about "my Father's house"; in Mark, a quote from Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11).

All four Gospels agree on the core: Jesus acted against the trade in the temple grounds, and the authorities saw it as a challenge to their authority.

deep.h: Six jars and a lot of wine
deep.b: Each jar held two or three "measures" (metrētēs, about 40 liters or 10 gallons), so the six held some 120–180 gallons (450–700 liters). That is far more than a village feast needed. The prophets pictured the coming age as a time when "the mountains will drip with sweet wine" (Amos 9:13), and 2 Baruch 29:5 imagines a vine with grapes that each produce a huge measure of wine. John's readers would hear abundance: the gift of God is not rationed. Some readers see in the number six, one short of seven, a hint that the old rites were incomplete; others think the number is simply what was there.

echoes: Genesis 49:10–12; Exodus 19:11–16; Isaiah 25:6; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Amos 9:13–14; Joel 3:18; Zechariah 14:21; Psalm 69:9; Mark 11:15–18; Mark 14:58; Mark 2:19–22; Matthew 21:12–13; Matthew 26:61; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Revelation 19:7–9

settings.when: during a village wedding feast at Cana, when the wine ran short
settings.why: Mary states a need, and Jesus pushes back: his actions are set by his "hour", the time fixed by his Father, not by family. Yet his mother tells the servants to obey him, and he acts. The exchange shows both his independence and her trust.
settings.readers: For John's readers the word "hour" pointed ahead to the cross, so the first sign already belongs to the story of his death and glory.

settings.to: Animal sellers and money changers, then "the Jews", the temple authorities who demanded a sign
settings.when: at Passover, in the crowded temple grounds
settings.why: Jesus claims the temple as "my Father's house" and challenges how it is run. Asked for proof of his authority, he gives a riddle: the sign will be a destroyed and rebuilt temple. The hearers take it of the building; later the disciples understood he meant his body raised on the third day.
settings.readers: If, as most scholars think, John's readers lived after AD 70, when the Romans had destroyed the temple, the scene told them that God's dwelling was not lost: it is found in the risen Jesus.
views: Most scholars think the Gospel was finished after the temple fell, so 2:19–21 would comfort readers who had lost it.
A few (Robinson, and others who date John early) think the scene was written while the temple stood, as a warning.

traditions.q: What does Mary's role at Cana mean for how Christians relate to her?
views: Mary notices the need and brings it to her Son, who acts at her word. The church sees here her intercession for believers, and her words "Whatever he says to you, do it" as her constant counsel; Christians may ask her prayers.
The Theotokos (God-bearer) intercedes for the faithful as she did at Cana, and the church honors her above all saints, while worship is given to God alone.

Mary is honored as a model of faith who trusted her Son even when he refused her. The Augsburg Confession teaches that saints are to be remembered and imitated, but not called upon for help, since Christ is the one mediator.

Jesus' answer "What does that have to do with me and you, woman?" shows that his mother had no authority over his work. Calvin read it as a correction. Mary is honored for her faith, but prayer is directed to God alone.
Mary is an example of faith and obedience, pointing others to Jesus, not a mediator. Most Baptists stress that the text says she directed the servants to him, not to herself.

traditions.q: Jesus made a great deal of good wine (2:10). May Christians drink alcohol?
views: Yes, in moderation. Wine is a good gift of God and is used in the Eucharist; drunkenness is a sin.
Yes. Wine is blessed at weddings and used in the Liturgy, though it is given up on many fast days.
Yes, as a gift of God to be used with thanksgiving and self-control.
The United Methodist Church allows but urges caution, recommending abstinence as a faithful witness, and uses unfermented grape juice for Communion, a practice begun by Methodists in the 1800s.

Southern Baptists have long urged total abstinence from alcohol, and their resolutions oppose its use. Some Baptists argue the Cana wine was ordinary wine but that modern conditions call for abstinence.
The Assemblies of God asks its ministers to abstain and urges members to do the same, citing the dangers of alcohol today.
Seventh-day Adventists abstain from alcohol as part of caring for the body as God's temple. Ellen G. White taught that the wine Jesus made at Cana was unfermented grape juice.

title: Born from above
sum: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader, comes to Jesus at night and calls him a teacher sent from God. Jesus answers that no one can see God's kingdom without being born "from above", a word that can also mean "again". Nicodemus takes it literally, and Jesus explains: the new birth comes from water and Spirit, as unseen and free as the wind. Then he speaks of the Son of Man who must be lifted up as Moses lifted up the bronze snake, so that all who believe may have eternal life. "This is how God loved the world: he gave his only Son" (3:16).

The scene then moves to the Judean countryside, where Jesus' disciples and John the Baptist are both baptizing. John's disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus. John answers with a picture: he is only the groom's friend, glad to hear the groom's voice. "He must keep growing, and I must keep getting smaller" (3:30). The chapter ends with a summary of the Gospel's message: the one from above speaks God's words, and the person who believes in the Son has eternal life.
readings: Read as a conversation

Nicodemus is a real person with real questions, and the scene shows how hard it was for a respected teacher to accept Jesus. He fades out of the conversation after 3:9, but he reappears in 7:50 and 19:39, each time a little bolder.
Read as a sermon

After 3:10 the dialogue becomes a monologue, and from 3:16 on many hear the evangelist's own voice. The chapter works as a compact summary of John's message: new birth, the cross, God's love, and judgment by one's response to the light.
Read as a debate about baptism

Water and washings run through the chapter (3:5, 22–26). Some readers think John is addressing disputes between followers of Jesus and followers of the Baptist, and between churches about baptism and the Spirit.

views.H: Nicodemus is a plausible Jerusalem figure, and the Talmud knows a rich Naqdimon in the city before AD 70. That Jesus and John baptized at the same time, side by side, is reported only here; most historians take it seriously, since it does not flatter Jesus. Aenon near Salim was placed by Eusebius in the Jordan valley south of Beth-shean.
views.C: Critical scholars debate where Jesus' words end (3:15 or 3:21) and whether 3:31–36 belongs to the Baptist or the narrator; some (Bultmann, Schnackenburg) proposed moving 3:31–36 to follow 3:21. Many see in the plural "we" and "you people" (3:7, 11) the voice of the later church arguing with the synagogue (Martyn).
views.L: The chapter is a classic Johannine misunderstanding: Nicodemus hears "born again" and thinks of his mother's womb. Double meanings carry the theology: anōthen (again/from above), pneuma (wind/Spirit), "lifted up" (raised on a cross/exalted). Night and light frame the scene (3:2, 19–21).
views.J: Nicodemus represents the best of Jewish learning, and the conversation draws on Israel's Scriptures: Ezekiel's new heart and Spirit, the bronze snake, the "only son" of Genesis 22. Rabbis later spoke of a convert as "like a newborn child" (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 22a), a possible background for "born again". Jewish readers note that 3:18 has been used to deny any hope for Jews who do not believe in Jesus, a reading many churches have since questioned.
views.T: 3:5 became the chief text for baptism as new birth in the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican traditions; revivalist Protestants made "born again" the name for personal conversion. 3:16, often called "the gospel in miniature" (a phrase commonly attributed to Luther), is probably the most quoted verse in the Bible. 3:30 was later linked to the Baptist's feast at midsummer, when the days begin to shorten.

deep.b:
Ancient Greek had no quotation marks, so every translation must decide how far Jesus' words run. Three options are common. To 3:21: the KJV with its later red-letter editions, and most modern English Bibles, keep the whole section as Jesus' words; this translation does too. To 3:15: many commentators (Schnackenburg, among others) think 3:16–21 is John's own reflection, and the RSV (1952) closed the quotation at 3:15, with a footnote that some continue it to 3:21, since it speaks of the Son in the third person, uses past tenses ("loved", "gave", "has entered") and sounds like 1 John. Blended: others say John deliberately lets his voice and Jesus' voice merge, as a witness who speaks in his master's words.

The question matters less than it seems. On any reading the words come with the Gospel's full authority. But it reminds readers that the punctuation of the Bible is an interpretation.

The early church read 3:5 almost unanimously of baptism: Justin Martyr (about AD 155) quotes "unless you are born again you will not enter the kingdom of heaven" while describing baptism (First Apology 61). This became the teaching of the Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran churches, and of the Anglican Prayer Book, which calls the baptized child "regenerate".

In the 1700s John Wesley and George Whitefield preached "the new birth" as a conscious inward change through faith, distinct from baptism, and the phrase became central to the evangelical revivals. In the 1970s "born-again Christian" became an American label for evangelicals. Today many churches hold both: God's new life is signed and given in baptism, and must be received and lived in personal faith.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Nicodemus sees the lifting up
deep.b: This is my own reading of the three Nicodemus scenes. In 3:14 Jesus tells Nicodemus, of all people, that the Son of Man must be lifted up like the snake on the pole, so that those who look may live. Nicodemus does not reply. The next time he speaks is to ask for Jesus to be heard fairly (7:50–51). The last time he appears, he comes with Joseph of Arimathea to take down the body of the one who has been lifted up (19:38–39). John notes there that he was the one who had first come at night. It may be that John means Nicodemus as the reader's example of someone who came to understand 3:14 only by standing at the cross, the one who heard about the lifted Son in the dark and finally looked at him in daylight.

echoes: Ezekiel 36:25–27; Ezekiel 37:9–14; Numbers 21:4–9; Genesis 22:2; Isaiah 52:13; Proverbs 30:4; Deuteronomy 30:12; Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20; 1:12–13; 7:50–52; 12:32–34; 19:39; Mark 2:19–20; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 1:3; 1 John 4:9–10; 1 John 5:1

settings.by: Jesus (and, in many readings, the narrator from 3:16)
settings.to: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader, probably a member of the Jerusalem council, and through him the group he spoke for ("we know", 3:2)
settings.when: at night, in Jerusalem, during or after the Passover of 2:13–25
settings.why: Nicodemus comes impressed by signs, as many did (2:23). Jesus tells him that signs and good teaching are not enough: a person needs a birth from God. A respected teacher of Israel is told he must begin again. The plural "you people" widens the challenge to all who, like him, admire Jesus from a safe distance.
settings.readers: For John's readers, Nicodemus stood for people who admired Jesus but kept it quiet, like the leaders of 12:42 who feared losing their place in the synagogue. If, as some think, such secret believers were among the first readers, Nicodemus was a figure they knew from the inside. The scene called them to come into the light.
views: Many (Carson, Keener) take it as a memory of an actual night conversation, reshaped in John's style.
Others (Martyn) read it at two levels: a story about Jesus and also the church's argument with synagogue teachers in John's day.

settings.to: His own disciples, who were upset that crowds were leaving John for Jesus
settings.when: in Judea, while both were baptizing
settings.why: To stop their rivalry. John insists that his role was given from heaven and that it was always to prepare for someone else. As the groom's friend, he finds his joy in the groom's success, not his own.
settings.readers: For readers who knew followers of John who had not followed Jesus (Acts 19:1–7), the Baptist's own words settled the question of rank.

settings.what: The one who comes from above
settings.by: Either John the Baptist, continuing, or the Gospel's narrator
settings.to: The Baptist's disciples, or the Gospel's readers
settings.why: To sum up what the chapter has said: Jesus comes from heaven, speaks God's words, has the Spirit without limit and has received all things from the Father, and the response to him decides between life and wrath.
settings.readers: These verses gather the Gospel's message into a few lines for any reader.
views: Some read the verses as John's continued testimony, as many older commentators read it.
Most modern translations close John's words at 3:30 and treat these verses as reflection, like 3:16–21.

traditions.q: Does "born from water and Spirit" (3:5) mean that baptism brings new birth?
views: Yes. Baptism is the sacrament of regeneration by water and the Spirit, and 3:5 shows it is necessary for salvation for those who have heard the gospel; God is not bound by his sacraments in other cases.
Yes. In baptism a person dies and rises with Christ and is born anew; chrismation, the gift of the Spirit, follows at once, even for infants.
Yes. Baptism is a "washing of regeneration" by which God works forgiveness and new birth through his word joined to water; faith receives it.
The Book of Common Prayer declares the baptized "regenerate" and quotes 3:5 in the service. Evangelical and Anglo-Catholic Anglicans interpret that language differently.
Baptism is a sign and seal of regeneration, not its cause; grace is not tied to the moment of baptism. Calvin thought "water" here means the Spirit's cleansing, not baptism directly.
Wesley taught that infants are born again in baptism, but that adults who have fallen away must be born again by faith; the new birth is an inward change by the Spirit.
No. The new birth is the Spirit's work received through faith, and baptism is the believer's public sign of it afterward; "water" refers to natural birth or the Spirit's cleansing.
Churches of Christ teach that baptism of believers by immersion is when God forgives sins and gives new birth, citing 3:5 with Acts 2:38.

traditions.q: Does "God loved the world" (3:16) mean Christ died to save every person, or the chosen?
views: Christ died for all people without exception, and God wills all to be saved; human freedom can refuse this love.
God's grace is truly for all, and Christ made satisfaction for the whole world. Those who are saved are saved by grace alone; those lost are lost by their own fault, not by God's decree.

God loves the world in a general way, but Christ's death was designed to save the elect, and secures their salvation (the Canons of Dort). Many Reformed read "world" as all kinds of people, or as the world in its rebellion.
God's grace is free in all and free for all. Christ died for every person, and prevenient grace makes each person able to respond.
Baptists are divided: most Southern Baptists hold that Christ died for all; Reformed Baptists, in the tradition of the 1689 Confession, hold particular redemption.

title: Living water in Samaria
sum: On the way north to Galilee, Jesus rests at Jacob's well near the Samaritan town of Sychar at noon and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. She is surprised: Jews and Samaritans kept apart. Jesus offers her "living water" that becomes a spring inside a person, leaping up to eternal life. He tells her about her five husbands, and she, sensing a prophet, raises the old dispute: Mount Gerizim or Jerusalem? Jesus answers that the hour is coming when the Father will be worshiped in spirit and truth, and then tells her plainly that he is the Messiah: "I am he" (4:26).

She leaves her water jar and brings her townspeople. Meanwhile Jesus tells the puzzled disciples that his food is to do the will of the one who sent him, and that the fields are already ripe. The Samaritans believe, first because of her testimony and then because of his words, and call him "the Savior of the world" (4:42). Back in Galilee, a royal official begs Jesus to heal his dying son. Jesus sends him home with a word, and the boy recovers at that very hour: the second sign at Cana.
readings: Read as a story of crossing boundaries

Jesus speaks with a woman, a Samaritan, and one with a complicated past, and she becomes a witness to her town. The chapter crosses lines of sex, ethnicity and religion that his disciples took for granted (4:27).
Read as a story about worship
The question at the center is where God is to be worshiped. Jesus moves it from the place to the person: true worship happens in the Spirit and in the truth that comes through him.
Read with chapter 3
Nicodemus, a respected Jewish man, comes at night and fades from view; the woman, an unnamed Samaritan, meets Jesus at noon and brings a town to him. The contrast seems deliberate.

views.H: Jacob's well and Sychar (Askar) are real places near Shechem, and Mount Gerizim with its ruined Samaritan temple stood above them. Josephus confirms that Galileans traveled through Samaria and that clashes sometimes broke out. The royal official most likely served Herod Antipas, who governed Galilee. The healing at a distance resembles the centurion story in Matthew and Luke.
views.C: Many scholars connect the chapter with a Christian mission to Samaria (Acts 8), and some think the Johannine community included Samaritan believers. The "second sign" (4:54) is often traced to a Signs Source. Scholars debate whether the five husbands have a symbolic meaning (Samaria's foreign gods).
views.L: The well scene borrows the shape of biblical betrothal stories (Isaac, Jacob, Moses), right after Jesus has been called the groom (3:29). The woman's understanding grows step by step (a Jew, sir, a prophet, the Messiah), while the disciples misunderstand about food. The chapter ends where chapter 2 began, at Cana.
views.J: Jesus speaks as a Jew ("salvation comes from the Jews", 4:22) and affirms Jerusalem's past role while announcing a new hour. Samaritans and Jews shared the Torah but disputed the holy place. Amy-Jill Levine and others caution against reading the woman as an outcast or Jewish customs as harsher than the evidence shows.
views.T: The Orthodox Church honors the woman as Saint Photini ("enlightened"), "equal to the apostles", and keeps a Sunday of the Samaritan Woman after Easter. Many preachers have taken her as a model of evangelism, and 4:23–24 has shaped Christian thinking about worship, from the Reformation's suspicion of shrines to Quaker silent worship. The harvest sayings (4:35–38) have been central to missionary preaching.

deep.b:
Samaritans and Jews both worshiped the God of Israel and kept the Torah, but they disagreed about the place God had chosen. The Samaritan Pentateuch names Mount Gerizim as the holy place, and Samaritans worshiped there. Excavations on the summit led by Yitzhak Magen found a sacred precinct from the mid-400s BC, thousands of coins and some hundreds of inscriptions; Josephus places the building of the temple in Alexander the Great's time (Antiquities 11.310–324). The Jewish king John Hyrcanus destroyed it, about 128 BC by Josephus' account (Antiquities 13.255–256) or about 111 BC by Magen's coin evidence, and bitterness grew on both sides. Jews later spoke of Samaritans as "Cutheans", foreigners; Samaritans called Jerusalem's temple a heresy.

Jesus' answer to the woman takes Jerusalem's side for the past (4:22) and then declares both places finished as the center of worship (4:21, 23). For John, the temple is now Jesus' body (2:21), so worship "in spirit and truth" is worship through him. Within a generation of this conversation, the Jerusalem temple was destroyed too (AD 70). A Samaritan community of about 900 people still celebrates Passover on Gerizim today.

Readers have painted her in very different colors. For much of church history she was the model sinner, exposed and forgiven: Augustine read her five husbands as the five senses. Modern scholars note that the story never mentions sin, forgiveness or repentance. She may have been widowed or divorced several times through no fault of her own, and "the one you have now" may have been a man who gave her a home without marriage. Her many questions show her as a serious conversation partner, the first person in John to whom Jesus says "I am".

What the story does say clearly is that she becomes a witness. She goes back to the town, tells what happened, and asks, "He couldn't be the Messiah, could he?" (4:29). Her testimony leads many to believe (4:39), and the townspeople then come to faith through Jesus' own words (4:42), the pattern John wants for all his readers.

echoes: Genesis 24:10–27; Genesis 29:1–12; Genesis 33:18–20; Genesis 48:22; Exodus 2:15–21; Deuteronomy 11:29; Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Joshua 24:32; 2 Kings 17:24–41; Jeremiah 2:13; Isaiah 12:3; Isaiah 55:1; Zechariah 14:8; Amos 9:13; 7:37–39; 2:1–11; Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10; Luke 10:2; Acts 8:4–25; 1 John 4:14

settings.by: Jesus and an unnamed Samaritan woman
settings.to: Each other, alone at the well
settings.when: at noon by Jacob's well near Sychar, while the disciples were buying food
settings.why: Jesus starts with a simple request and moves the conversation from well water to living water, from her life to true worship, and finally to who he is. The woman is not a passive listener: she argues, asks about Jacob and the holy mountain, and voices the Samaritan hope of a coming one.
settings.readers: For readers in churches that included Jews and other peoples (and, some scholars think, Samaritan believers), the scene showed that the dispute over holy places no longer divided them: all worship the Father through Jesus.
views: A memory of a real meeting
Many (Keener, Carson) think a historical encounter lies behind the story, perhaps remembered among Samaritan Christians.
Others (Brown, Martyn) think the story was shaped to support the church's later mission in Samaria and the inclusion of Samaritan believers.

settings.to: His disciples, as they urged him to eat
settings.when: while the woman had gone to the town and its people were coming out
settings.why: The disciples think of food; Jesus speaks of the work God has given him. Pointing to the Samaritans on their way, he tells them the harvest is ready now, and that they are being sent to reap where others did the hard work.
settings.readers: For later missionaries and churches, the saying explained how they could gather a harvest they had not planted, and gave honor to those who sowed before them.
views: The others are Jesus and the woman
Many read the "others" (4:38) as Jesus and the woman, whose work the disciples now reap.
Some (Cullmann, Brown) think the saying reflects the later Samaritan mission of Philip and the Hellenist believers (Acts 8).

settings.what: "Come and look at a man": the woman and the townspeople
settings.by: The Samaritan woman, then the people of Sychar
settings.to: The people of her town, and then the woman herself
settings.when: after her talk with Jesus at the well, and again after he had stayed two days in the town
settings.why: The woman's words are an invitation and a cautious question ("He couldn't be the Messiah, could he?"), not a claim she insists on. Her testimony brings the town to Jesus. After hearing him for themselves, the townspeople tell her that their faith no longer rests on her talk, and they confess him as "the Savior of the world".
settings.readers: For John's readers, the scene modeled how faith passes from a witness's word to a person's own meeting with Jesus, which is what the Gospel itself hopes to do (20:30–31).
views: Most readers see the townspeople's words as the natural growth of faith, not a put-down of the woman, whose witness began it (4:39).
Some feminist interpreters hear the townspeople's "no longer because of your talk" as dismissive of her, and note that John still credits her testimony.

settings.to: The official, most likely a man in the service of Herod Antipas (some identify him with the centurion of Matthew 8), and the Galileans standing by ("you people", 4:48)
settings.when: at Cana, after Jesus' return from Judea and Samaria
settings.why: The father asks Jesus to come and heal his son. Jesus first warns that faith built only on wonders is weak, then gives a word instead of a visit. The man trusts the word and goes; the healing is confirmed at the very hour.
settings.readers: John's readers had never seen Jesus. The story showed them that his word works at a distance, and that trusting it is real faith (20:29).
